title: Direct identifiability from rich biometric and location telemetry shared by the wearer
description: By continuously providing heart-rate patterns, GPS position, timestamps, and activity data to the wearable device, the wearer becomes directly or indirectly identifiable. The act of sharing this combination of data enables singling out of the individual, especially when location/time traces reveal home, work, or routine.
assumptions: Assumes the wearable device can associate incoming telemetry with a persistent device or account context.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context gives applicable threat types but not detailed node ids.

title: Linkability of multiple observations about the same wearer at the point of collection
description: Continuous sensor capture causes multiple telemetry records over time to be linkable to the same wearer. Repeated heart-rate, step-count, GPS, and timestamp data can be correlated into a persistent behavioral profile even before further downstream processing.
assumptions: Assumes records are collected under a stable device/session context rather than as fully unlinkable one-off samples.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ.

title: Linkability through transmission metadata on the telemetry flow
description: The telemetry flow itself may expose stable communication metadata, timing patterns, and repeated transmissions that allow linking successive sensor uploads to the same wearer/device. Even if payload fields were minimized, the recurring flow can support correlation.
assumptions: Assumes the device communication channel exposes persistent or observable metadata such as device identifiers, packet timing, or session continuity.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate.

title: Identification via in-transit location and temporal metadata
description: Data in transit includes or implies GPS coordinates and timestamps, which can identify the wearer by revealing habitual locations and movement patterns. Observers of the flow may infer identity from home/work locations or unique travel routines.
assumptions: Assumes the telemetry is observable in transit by relevant parties or intermediaries and contains location/time information in readable or inferable form.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate.

title: Detectability of sensitive states by the wearable device upon receipt
description: Once the wearable device receives continuous heart-rate, activity, and location telemetry, it can detect sensitive states or events such as exercise habits, sleep/wake cycles, presence at particular places, or unusual physiological episodes. The recipient's processing makes the existence of these conditions detectable.
assumptions: Assumes the device software processes or stores the telemetry in a way that reveals such states.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement.

title: Disclosure of highly sensitive health and location data at the wearable device
description: The wearable device receives and may store highly sensitive telemetry including biometric measurements and precise location history. If the device exposes this data to unauthorized local apps, users, debuggers, or later interfaces, confidentiality is compromised at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the device stores or makes the received telemetry accessible beyond the minimum trusted processing boundary.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate and depends on the detailed LINDDUN Pro tree used.

title: Unawareness of the extent of continuous sensing and inference by the wearable device
description: The wearer may be unaware that continuous collection of heart rate, steps, GPS, and timestamps enables detailed inference about routines, health, and whereabouts once the device receives and processes the data. This creates a privacy threat if the destination does not make the scope and consequences of collection clear.
assumptions: Assumes insufficient notice or understandable feedback is provided to the wearer about ongoing collection and resulting inferences.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate.

title: Non-compliance risk from collecting more telemetry than necessary
description: Receiving continuous GPS, timestamps, heart rate, and step counts may exceed what is necessary for a specific wearable function, creating a risk that the destination's collection and processing are not compliant with data minimization, purpose limitation, or consent requirements.
assumptions: Assumes no clearly justified purpose, valid consent, or minimization controls for all collected fields at this stage.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate and depends on applicable legal/regulatory context.

title: Excessive disclosure of detailed activity and location data to the companion app
description: The wearable device shares rich sensor batches including exercise sessions, GPS traces, device identifier, and timestamps with the companion app. If all fields are not strictly necessary for the app feature being used, the device's act of sending them constitutes avoidable disclosure of personal data beyond data minimization.
assumptions: Assumes some synced fields or granularity (e.g., precise GPS traces, persistent device id, exact timestamps) may exceed what is necessary for core synchronization.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best-fit judgement for explicit, avoidable disclosure/minimization at the source; retrieved context confirms Dd applicability but not the exact subtree citation.

title: Identification via device identifier and precise telemetry in transit
description: The flow contains a device id together with GPS traces and timestamps. Even if the person's name is absent, these attributes can identify or single out the user when observed on the wire or correlated with other data.
assumptions: Assumes the device id is persistent or otherwise stable across syncs, and that GPS/timestamp precision is sufficient to single out an individual.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate; applicability of Identification on this flow is high given the data categories.

title: Linkability of multiple sync events and datasets
description: Repeated syncs carrying the same device id plus timestamps allow records from different exercise sessions to be linked to the same user/device over time. This enables construction of longitudinal behavior profiles across batches.
assumptions: Assumes the identifier remains stable across sessions or that quasi-identifiers in the payload are sufficient for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is approximate; threat selection is based on classic linkability from stable identifiers and repeated observations.

title: Detectability of user activity patterns from sync metadata
description: The existence, timing, size, and frequency of synchronization events can reveal when the user exercised, traveled, or was active, even without inspecting full payload contents. This makes sensitive behavior detectable from the flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes an observer can access traffic metadata or infer payload size/timing characteristics.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate; detectability is grounded mainly in traffic metadata rather than payload semantics.

title: Linking synced wearable data with other app-held data
description: On receipt, the companion app can combine exercise sessions, GPS traces, timestamps, and device id with account, phone, or other app data, enabling broader linkage of datasets about the same person than is necessary for simple synchronization.
assumptions: Assumes the app has access to additional identifiers or contextual data beyond this flow.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate; destination-side linkage risk depends on the app's broader data holdings.

title: Over-collection or retention of precise synced data by the companion app
description: The companion app may receive and store precise GPS traces, timestamps, and persistent device identifiers at full fidelity, even where coarser or shorter-lived data would suffice. Receiving and retaining such detailed data creates avoidable disclosure at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the app stores or further processes the full synced payload rather than immediately minimizing it.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate; retrieved context supports Data Disclosure/minimization concerns but not this precise node.

title: Unawareness of the extent of data imported into the app
description: Users may not realize that syncing transfers precise GPS traces, exact timestamps, and a persistent device identifier into the companion app, nor understand the resulting inferences and retention implications. This creates a risk that processing occurs without adequate user awareness.
assumptions: Assumes the app's notices or sync UX do not clearly explain the categories, precision, and consequences of synced data.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree citation is approximate; unawareness depends on the actual transparency and consent UX.

title: User may be unaware of the privacy implications of manually entering sensitive health data
description: The wearer manually shares calorie intake, meal details, and weight with the companion app. These data are health- and lifestyle-related and can be highly sensitive. A privacy threat arises if the user is not adequately informed, at the moment of entry, about what data are collected, how they will be used, whether they will be combined with other data, and with whom they may be shared.
assumptions: The app collects and retains the entered data beyond transient display and may use it for analytics, personalization, or onward sharing.

title: Companion app can detect sensitive habits and health patterns from logged entries
description: By receiving structured logs of meals, calorie intake, and weight, the companion app can infer sensitive aspects of the user's behavior and health status, such as dieting behavior, eating patterns, weight changes, or possible medical conditions. This constitutes detectability of sensitive personal attributes at the destination.
assumptions: The app stores or processes the entries in a way that makes such patterns observable to the app provider or app components.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement; the retrieved context did not provide a more specific detectability node for this case.

title: Companion app can link manual nutrition and weight logs to the user's identity or profile
description: The destination process may associate the manually entered calorie, meal, and weight data with the user's account, device identifier, or other profile data. This enables linking these sensitive entries across sessions and with other datasets, increasing privacy risk.
assumptions: The app maintains a persistent account, device identifier, or profile that can be associated with the submitted entries.
uncertainty_note: Specific threat-tree node id may vary by LINDDUN Pro version; chosen as a best-fit generic linkability node.

title: Companion app can identify the wearer from submitted diet and weight entries
description: If the companion app receives the entries together with account, device, or session information, the data may be directly or indirectly attributable to the wearer. Even if the content itself is not uniquely identifying, the receiving process can identify the individual by combining it with existing identifiers.
assumptions: The app has access to account, device, or session identifiers when receiving the data.
uncertainty_note: Specific threat-tree node id is a best-fit generic identifiability node because the retrieved context did not include the detailed identification subtree.

title: User may lack sufficient control over retention, deletion, or downstream use of logged entries
description: Once the wearer submits calorie, meal, and weight data to the companion app, the destination process may not provide adequate means to edit, delete, restrict processing, or prevent secondary use of those entries. This creates a non-compliance risk with privacy principles and data protection obligations.
assumptions: The app stores the submitted entries and may not fully support user rights or purpose limitation.
uncertainty_note: This is framed as a destination-side non-compliance risk; applicability depends on actual app controls and governance.

title: App writes more health data than necessary to the store
description: The mobile app may disclose excessive personal health data to the health log store by sending full calorie intake, weight history, and exercise-session details when only a subset or lower granularity is needed for the intended feature. This creates avoidable disclosure at the moment of sharing from the source process.
assumptions: Assumes some app features could operate with less detailed, less frequent, or partially aggregated health-log data than what is written.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality structure; exact subnode may vary by catalog version.

title: Health-log writes can be linked to the same user over time via flow metadata
description: Repeated write operations from the companion app to the store can expose stable identifiers or consistent metadata such as account ID, device ID, session token, timestamps, or record structure, enabling correlation of multiple submissions as belonging to the same individual over time.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries stable identifiers or otherwise correlatable metadata alongside the health-log payload.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability depends on whether stable identifiers or correlatable metadata are present on this flow.

title: Health-log payload or metadata may identify the user in transit
description: The data flow may contain directly identifying fields or quasi-identifiers, such as account identifiers, precise timestamps, rare exercise patterns, or detailed weight history, that allow the recipient or an observer with access to the flow to identify the data subject.
assumptions: Assumes the transmitted records include direct identifiers or combinations of attributes sufficient for singling out a user.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; identification may also arise indirectly from combinations of health attributes rather than explicit identifiers.

title: Store retains detailed health logs in an unnecessarily disclosive form
description: Upon receipt, the health log store may persist detailed calorie, weight, and exercise records at full fidelity or for longer than necessary, increasing avoidable disclosure risk if the data is later accessed, repurposed, or breached.
assumptions: Assumes the datastore stores raw or long-lived records rather than minimizing, aggregating, or deleting them according to necessity.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is best-effort; this is a destination-side disclosure/minimization concern rather than a transport issue.

title: Health logs may be stored or reused for purposes users do not expect
description: The destination datastore may enable secondary use of detailed health logs beyond the user's expected purpose, such as analytics, profiling, or feature expansion, without sufficient transparency or alignment with the original collection context.
assumptions: Assumes purpose limitation is not strictly enforced once data reaches the store and that downstream consumers may access the stored logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; threat depends on actual governance and purpose-limitation controls around DS1.

title: Storage of health logs may exceed or diverge from the user's consent
description: The datastore may receive and keep categories or granularity of health data that the user did not explicitly consent to, or continue storing them after consent withdrawal, creating a non-compliance risk tied to this write operation.
assumptions: Assumes consent is the relevant legal basis for at least some of these health-log writes and that consent scope/withdrawal may not be enforced at write time.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate and applicability depends on the system's legal basis and consent-management design.

title: Excessive collection and transfer of precise location traces
description: The mobile app writes GPS traces with timestamps to the history store. Precise, timestamped location history is highly sensitive personal data; collecting and sending full traces may disclose more detail than is necessary for the app's purpose if coarse location, reduced frequency, or on-device processing would suffice.
assumptions: Assumes the app's purpose may not require continuous precise historical tracking at full granularity.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality structure; exact subnode may vary by catalog version.

title: Linkability through persistent location-history uploads
description: A stream of GPS points with timestamps can be linked to the same device/user over time, enabling correlation of trips, routines, home/work locations, and repeated visits. Even if direct identifiers are absent, the trajectory itself is often uniquely linkable.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong because mobility traces are well known to be highly linkable.

title: Identifiability from unique mobility patterns in transit
description: Timestamped GPS traces can identify an individual because home/work pairs, habitual routes, and rare visits are often unique. Thus the data flow itself carries enough quasi-identifying information to single out the user.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; identifiability from mobility traces is strongly supported in privacy literature though the precise catalog node may differ.

title: Over-retention of detailed location history
description: Once received, the location history store may retain precise traces and timestamps longer than necessary. Long-term storage increases disclosure risk because historical movements reveal sensitive habits, visits, and associations.
assumptions: Assumes retention limits, aggregation, or deletion policies may be absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort for storage/retention-related disclosure; exact subnode may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Secondary use of stored location history beyond the original purpose
description: The destination store enables later analytics or sharing of historical location data for purposes beyond providing the companion app's core function, such as profiling, marketing, or law-enforcement response, without the user's compatible expectation.
assumptions: Assumes governance and purpose-limitation controls are not fully enforced at the store or downstream consumers.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat depends on broader system governance but is a genuine risk for persistent location-history stores.

title: Insufficient transparency/consent for storing historical location traces
description: Storing detailed GPS history with timestamps may exceed what users reasonably understand or have specifically consented to, especially if retention period, precision, or downstream uses are not clearly communicated and controllable.
assumptions: Assumes consent/notice may be bundled, unclear, or not granular for historical storage.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; applicability depends on the system's notice and consent design, which is not fully specified.

title: Over-disclosure of longitudinal health logs to analytics
description: The data store shares calorie, weight, and exercise logs across sessions with the analytics service. Because these are sensitive health-related data and longitudinal records, the flow may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for the stated health-condition analysis, violating data minimization.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics use case could be fulfilled with a reduced subset, aggregation, or shorter retention window rather than full cross-session raw logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on data-disclosure/minimization semantics; exact subnode may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Linkability through persistent cross-session health-log transfer
description: This flow explicitly carries logs across sessions to the analytics service. Persistent identifiers, timestamps, or stable record structure in the transferred dataset can allow records from multiple sessions to be linked to the same individual, enabling longitudinal profiling beyond what data subjects may expect.
assumptions: Assumes the transferred records contain stable account, device, or temporal attributes that permit correlation across sessions.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode is inferred from standard linkability concepts; citation may be approximate.

title: Identifiability from detailed health and activity logs in transit
description: Even if direct identifiers are absent, combinations of weight history, calorie intake, exercise patterns, and timestamps can single out or re-identify a person when received by the analytics service or combined with other available data.
assumptions: Assumes quasi-identifiers or distinctive behavioral patterns are present in the transferred logs.
uncertainty_note: Subnode selection is best-effort; identifiability clearly applies but exact numbering may differ.

title: Detectability of a user's health-condition analysis participation
description: By receiving and processing these health logs, the analytics service may make it observable that a particular user is undergoing health-condition analysis or belongs to a health-related cohort. The mere presence of such records at the destination can reveal sensitive involvement even before full content analysis.
assumptions: Assumes access patterns, job queues, labels, or downstream outputs expose that the user is part of a health-analysis workflow.
uncertainty_note: Detectability is plausible here, but depends on whether participation in this analytics process is itself observable.

title: Secondary disclosure through derived health-condition inferences
description: The analytics service may derive sensitive conclusions about health conditions from the received logs. These inferred attributes can constitute additional personal data disclosure beyond the original raw logs, especially if stored, shared, or used for broader purposes.
assumptions: Assumes P3 generates or exposes inferred health-condition indicators, risk scores, or categorizations from the input logs.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd subnode is approximate; threat is grounded in implicit/derived disclosure described in LINDDUN guidance.

title: Unawareness of cross-session health analytics use
description: Data subjects may not be adequately aware that their calorie, weight, and exercise logs are read across sessions for health-condition analysis. If this use is not transparent, users may not understand the scope, sensitivity, or consequences of the processing.
assumptions: Assumes notices or UI do not clearly explain this specific analytics purpose and the cross-session nature of the processing.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness depends on the surrounding transparency mechanisms, which are not described in the flow alone.

title: Potential non-compliance in processing sensitive health-related data
description: The analytics service processes longitudinal health-related logs for condition analysis, which may trigger heightened legal obligations such as explicit purpose limitation, minimization, special-category data safeguards, and lawful-basis requirements. If these are not met, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the calorie, weight, and exercise logs are treated as personal data and may reveal health status under applicable law.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations are jurisdiction-dependent; exact legal trigger may vary.

title: Excessive disclosure of cross-session location history to analytics
description: The location history store discloses detailed historical location data across sessions to the analytics service. Sharing raw or fine-grained history may exceed what is strictly necessary to derive daily routine and movement patterns, creating avoidable disclosure of sensitive personal data.
assumptions: DS2 provides detailed or long-retention location traces rather than minimized, aggregated, or filtered data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Linkability through cross-session correlation of location records
description: The analytics service explicitly queries location history across sessions to derive routines and movement patterns. This processing links records from multiple sessions belonging to the same individual or household, enabling correlation of behavior over time beyond isolated session use.
assumptions: P3 can associate records across sessions using stable identifiers, account context, device identifiers, or equivalent correlators.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; the threat clearly concerns linkability via correlation across sessions.

title: Identifiability from unique movement patterns
description: Daily routines and movement patterns derived from historical location traces can uniquely characterize a person. Even if direct identifiers are absent, home/work locations and repeated trajectories may allow the analytics service to identify or single out individuals.
assumptions: Location traces are sufficiently granular or long-lived to reveal distinctive patterns such as home/work anchors or rare routes.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; identifiability from quasi-identifying mobility patterns is the core concern.

title: Detectability of sensitive habits and presence patterns
description: By analyzing historical location data, the recipient can detect whether a person visited particular places, was present at certain times, or follows recurring habits. This makes otherwise less observable behaviors detectable from the transferred data.
assumptions: The queried history includes timestamps and place granularity sufficient to infer visits, absences, or recurring routines.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; threat is detectability of behaviors/presence from location-history analysis.

title: Implicit disclosure of sensitive inferences from movement-pattern analytics
description: The analytics service derives daily routine and movement patterns from raw location history. These derived insights can implicitly disclose sensitive information such as home address, workplace, religious practice, health visits, political activity, or other intimate habits that were not explicitly provided as separate data fields.
assumptions: P3 stores, exposes, or otherwise uses the inferred patterns, and the underlying traces include visits or trajectories revealing sensitive places or behaviors.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode is best-judgement; the threat is implicit disclosure through inference from disclosed location data.

title: Unawareness of secondary analytics use of location history
description: Individuals may be unaware that their location history is queried across sessions to infer routines and movement patterns, especially if they expect location data to support immediate functionality rather than longitudinal behavioral profiling.
assumptions: Notices, consent flows, or just-in-time explanations do not clearly communicate this cross-session analytics purpose.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat depends on whether transparency about this secondary use is insufficient.

title: Non-compliant secondary use and over-processing of location history
description: Using historical location data across sessions to derive routines may be incompatible with purpose limitation, data minimization, storage limitation, or consent/legal-basis requirements if not strictly necessary and properly justified. The destination's processing can therefore create a compliance risk.
assumptions: The analytics purpose is secondary to the original collection purpose or lacks a clear legal basis, necessity assessment, or adequate safeguards.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; compliance assessment depends on jurisdiction and documented legal basis.

title: Inference results may reveal sensitive health information beyond what is necessary for app functionality
description: The analytics service shares inferred insights such as health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags with the mobile app. These outputs can disclose sensitive health inferences about the user, potentially exceeding what is necessary for the immediate user-facing purpose or exposing particularly sensitive categories of personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the inferred insights are privacy-sensitive health data and that not all returned fields are strictly necessary for every app interaction.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree granularity.

title: In-transit analytics results can identify the user through sensitive personalized health insights
description: Even if direct identifiers are minimized, the content and metadata of the returned analytics results may be sufficiently unique to identify or single out the user, especially when combined with device, account, or session context on the flow.
assumptions: Assumes the flow is associated with an authenticated app session or otherwise linkable communication context.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifying sub-node is not present in the retrieved context; citation is based on general LINDDUN identifying threats.

title: Returned insights may enable profiling and linkage to group membership
description: Risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags can reveal that the user belongs to a health-related or behavior-related group. Such inferred group membership can be linked with other observations or datasets, enabling profiling beyond the immediate transaction.
assumptions: Assumes the insights encode traits or patterns that correlate with recognizable cohorts or conditions.

title: Users may be unaware that the app receives and presents inferred health-condition risks
description: When the mobile app receives inferred insights from the analytics service, users may not understand that these are derived predictions or risk scores rather than raw observations, nor that such inferences are being generated and processed at all. This can undermine informed expectations and meaningful control.
assumptions: Assumes the app UX does not clearly explain the existence, nature, and implications of inferred analytics outputs.
uncertainty_note: Exact U sub-node chosen by best judgement because no unawareness node was included in the retrieved context.

title: Displaying and storing inferred health insights in the app may create compliance gaps if privacy and security controls are insufficient
description: Because the app receives potentially sensitive inferred health data, inadequate controls around presentation, local storage, access control, retention, or downstream sharing can create non-compliance with privacy and cybersecurity obligations. This non-compliance derives from the underlying disclosure, identifying, and unawareness risks associated with the flow.
assumptions: Assumes inferred health insights are regulated or otherwise high-risk personal data and that the app may persist or further process them.

title: Sensitive inferred health-risk indicators are disclosed to the user device/user context
description: The app actively shares highly sensitive inferred condition indicators and trend information (eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals) with the external entity. title: In-transit dashboard content can identify the user as having specific health risks
description: Data transmitted in this flow contains or strongly implies inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals. If intercepted or observable in transit, the content can identify the wearer as a person associated with particular health conditions or risks.
assumptions: The flow traverses device/app communication channels where interception, logging, or exposure of payloads/metadata is possible.
uncertainty_note: Applies mainly if transport/session protections or local IPC protections are weak; exact transport architecture is not specified.

title: Repeated dashboard updates enable linkability of sensitive health events over time
description: Trend displays and recurring inferred-condition updates on this flow may allow observations across sessions to be linked to the same wearer/device, revealing longitudinal patterns about health status evolution and behavior.
assumptions: An observer can correlate repeated transmissions, timestamps, device identifiers, or stable session characteristics.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement tree node; exact metadata fields are not provided.

title: User may be unaware of how inferred condition indicators are generated and what they mean
description: On receipt of the dashboard output, the wearer may not understand that the displayed trends are probabilistic inferences rather than diagnoses, what input data drove them, how accurate they are, or what secondary privacy implications follow from viewing/storing them on the device.

description: Because this flow presents inferred health information, inadequate transparency, explanation, consent/appropriate legal basis, or insufficient safeguards for special-category data could create regulatory non-compliance. uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and product context; tree node id is best-judgement.

title: Excessive disclosure of full health and location dataset to third-party cloud provider
description: The Health Analytics Service shares the full health and location dataset, along with analytics data and models, with an external cloud hosting provider for hosting and replication. Sending the full dataset to a third party may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for the hosting purpose, especially given the sensitivity of health and location data.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud provider is a separate controller/processor boundary and that not all raw personal data elements are strictly required in identifiable form for hosting or replication.

description: Upon receipt, the cloud hosting provider stores and replicates the analytics data, models, and full health/location dataset. Replication and provider-side handling can expand the set of systems, personnel, regions, or subprocessors with access to sensitive personal data, creating avoidable disclosure risk beyond the primary analytics service.
assumptions: Assumes replication may involve multiple storage locations, administrative domains, or subprocessors under the provider's control.

title: Identifiability of individuals in transit due to direct or rich quasi-identifiers
description: The transferred dataset contains full health and location data, which is highly likely to include direct identifiers or combinations of quasi-identifiers that make individuals identifiable during transmission. Even if names are absent, the richness of health and location records can enable singling out of data subjects.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset is not fully anonymised before transfer.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node is a best-fit estimate for identifiability from data content in transit.

title: Linkability of health and location records with analytics artifacts
description: Combining health records, location histories, analytics data, and models on the same transfer enables the recipient or an observer with access to the flow to link multiple records and contexts to the same individual or cohort. This can connect sensitive behavioural, medical, and movement patterns across datasets.
assumptions: Assumes analytics data/models preserve references, features, embeddings, or cohort structure derived from the underlying individuals.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; the threat is linkability created by transferring multiple correlated datasets/artifacts together.

description: Once the cloud provider receives the full health and location dataset and related analytics artifacts, data subjects may be unaware of or unable to reasonably foresee provider-side processing such as operational analytics, debugging, security monitoring, backup management, or subprocessor involvement. This creates a detectability/unawareness gap regarding how their sensitive data is handled.

If the transfer, replication scope, retention, or geographic distribution is not properly constrained, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes special-category data obligations apply and that contractual, geographic, retention, and processor controls may be incomplete or insufficiently specified.
